text:
The faint, phosphorescent glow from a patch of damp on the wall, near the forgotten portrait, pulsed faintly, like a sick heart. His mind, a ledger of horrors he hadn’t chosen to keep, flipped back to the Peterson cabin. Scorched earth. A child’s toy. Iris. The archives held ghosts, but the bay held bodies. The name L. Huang, silent partner to Thorne’s slow-motion demolition, still echoed in the hollow space between David’s temples. It was time to move. Time to trade faded ledgers for scorched earth.

He pushed through the heavy oak doors, the silence outside pressing in, thick and suffocating. It was less a quiet, more a sudden, town-wide ground stop. Not even the usual murmur of the sea reached his ears. The familiar coastal wind had died, the distant cry of gulls was gone. Even the low, persistent growl of the hum seemed to have retreated, leaving behind a vacuum where the town's living breath used to be. Every clock he passed, including the grand, stopped timepiece in the main hall, registered 7:56:17, an impossible freeze, a digital stutter in the fabric of Blackwood Bay.

Then the building groaned. Not the familiar, low thrum, but a sharp, deep-seated jolt, a physical cough from the earth’s throat that made the ancient stone groan. Dust rained from the high ceilings, settling on his shoulders like a fine ash. The earth beneath his feet wasn't breathing; it was coughing, trying to expel something that had been stuck in its throat for twenty years. The Peterson cabin called to him, a promise of answers in the scorched earth, a story waiting to be written, or perhaps, already told.
